children: SpaceX
said Thursday that any merger with Tesla
would require approval from Elon Musk, who controls the rocket and artificial intelligence company, even as both companies have established independent committees to evaluate a potential combination.
In its quarterly
, SpaceX

said its special committee hasn't reached a decision on a merger. Any agreement would need the endorsement of the committee, the company's board and its controlling shareholder. Musk has stepped aside from negotiations because of his interests in both companies.
"Because I'm a conflicted party, I can't actually be in the discussions of the special committees," Musk said during SpaceX's
quarterly earnings call.

The disclosure highlights a central challenge in a potential merger valued at approximately $3.5 trillion: protecting the interests of shareholders in two publicly traded companies dominated by the same billionaire. Investors are likely to scrutinize how the businesses are valued, the ownership stakes they would receive and whether independent directors can negotiate terms without undue influence from Musk.
Musk, who owns nearly 20% of Tesla
and controls voting rights at SpaceX

, said Tuesday that combining the companies would be a good idea. However, his public endorsement has raised concerns among some people involved in the discussions that shareholder scrutiny could complicate negotiations, according to several media reports.
The companies already have substantial commercial ties. SpaceX
disclosed that it purchased $151 million of Tesla

Megapack energy-storage products during the third quarter, bringing purchases during the first nine months of 2026 to $480 million. The filing also reported purchases of $506 million in Megapacks and $131 million in Cybertrucks as of December 31, 2025. The Cybertrucks were purchased at manufacturer's suggested retail prices.
Those transactions illustrate potential operational advantages of bringing the companies together. Tesla's
energy-storage technology could support SpaceX's

expanding data-center infrastructure, while a merger could simplify capital allocation and coordination of engineering resources across their artificial intelligence, energy and manufacturing operations.
The potential combination would unite companies with substantial investment requirements. Tesla
on Wednesday reduced its annual capital expenditure forecast to approximately $20 billion from more than $25 billion, while SpaceX
expects to spend $35 billion to $40 billion in the fourth quarter alone.
SpaceX's

filing showed that its capital expenditures totaled $19.6 billion during the third quarter, including $16.4 billion in its Super Intelligence division. The company also reported $51.3 billion in cash and cash equivalents and $38.6 billion in marketable securities at September 30, giving it substantial financial resources as it considers another major transaction.
A merger could also face national security scrutiny. SpaceX
provides launch and communications services to the U.S. government, including military and intelligence customers, while Tesla
maintains major manufacturing operations in China. The companies' international operations and government relationships could complicate regulatory reviews.
SpaceX

, which acquired Musk's xAI business earlier this year, has already expanded beyond its traditional rocket and satellite operations. Its artificial intelligence division includes Grok, social media platform X and coding software company Cursor, which SpaceX
acquired in August in a transaction involving $42.5 billion in purchase consideration.
For now, SpaceX
cautioned that negotiations might not produce an agreement and that its special committee could reject a transaction if it determines the terms wouldn't serve shareholders' interests.

title: SpaceX says Tesla merger needs Musk’s approval, discloses megapack purchases
